title: Timber floor cleaning and finish limits
audience: Cleaners working on timber floors with a sealed or oiled finish.
learningOutcomes: Identify whether a timber floor is sealed, oiled or unfinished before cleaning.
Use a method and product that suit the finish, with minimal moisture.
Stop and refer when the finish is worn, lifting or damaged.

instruction.heading: Finish first
instruction.body: The finish decides the method, so identify it before any product or water goes on the floor. A sealed timber floor has a film on the surface that resists water and most everyday soil. An oiled floor has oil or an oil-and-wax finish worked into the wood, so it is more sensitive to products that strip oil and to water that stays on the surface. An unfinished or raw timber floor has no protective layer, so it takes up water and product quickly. Even a sealed floor still needs a moisture-limited method, because water that stands at the edges and joints can get underneath the finish. Sources of information include the installer's or finisher's records, the strata or property manager's file and any maintenance history. Where those are not available, use a simple test in an inconspicuous spot. Apply a small amount of clean water and watch whether it beads, slowly darkens or soaks in. Beading suggests a sealed surface. Darkening or soaking suggests an oiled or raw surface. Treat the result as an indicator, and record the uncertainty if the answer is not clear.

instruction.heading: Method and product limits
instruction.body:
Use a damp-mop method with minimal moisture. A mop is damp when it is wrung until it is barely wet and does not drip when lifted. Work in small sections, along the grain where practical, and do not let the cloth or the mop sit in one place. Dry the section promptly with a clean microfibre cloth before you move on. Avoid steam, flooding and any method that pushes water into the seams or the edges. Keep the work area ventilated where a product has an odour, and follow the product label for dilution and contact time.

Use only products that the timber, the finish and your business have approved. Mild, pH-neutral cleaners made for timber are the usual starting point. Avoid ammonia-based cleaners, solvent-based products, abrasive pads and oil soaps on a sealed floor unless the product is approved for that finish, because these can cloud, soften or strip the finish. On an oiled floor, avoid products that are designed to strip finishes. Test the product on an inconspicuous area before wider use, and watch the area for a while after it dries.

Do not sand, screen, strip, recoat or re-oil a floor as part of routine cleaning. Those tasks change the finish and the surface of the wood. They are specialist finishing work, and a cleaner who carries them out outside a defined scope creates a dispute about what the work did.

instruction.heading: When to stop and refer
instruction.body:
Stop wet cleaning and refer the floor when you see any of the following: the finish is worn through to bare wood, boards are lifting at the edges or ends, boards are cupping or crowning, water is pooling on the surface, dark marks are spreading after a damp clean, or a stain does not respond to the approved method after a test. These signs can mean moisture has entered the timber, and more water will make them worse.

Record the condition with dated photographs taken in shade and under a light held low across the surface. Note the area, the signs you observed, the method you used and the moisture steps you took. Tell the client that the floor needs assessment by a qualified person, and that you cannot promise to restore the finish or remove the stain. Do not describe a floor as restored, sealed or repaired unless you carried out and recorded that work under a defined scope.

procedure: Identify the finish from records, or from a water-drop test in an inconspicuous spot, and record the result.
Check the boards for lifting, cupping, worn finish, pooling and dark marks before any water is used.
Choose a pH-neutral product approved for timber and for the finish, and confirm the label and SDS are on hand.
Wring the mop until it is barely damp, and clean in small sections, along the grain where practical.
Dry each section promptly with a clean microfibre cloth, and avoid steam, flooding and standing water.
Test the product on an inconspicuous area before wider use, and watch it dry.
Stop and refer for worn finish, lifting or cupping boards, pooling, or stains that do not respond. Record with photographs.

workedExamples.situation: A timber floor with an oiled finish shows dark marks after a damp mop, and the boards near the back door are slightly cupped.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before you clean any further?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop wet cleaning. The cupping and the dark marks suggest moisture has entered the timber. Dry the area with a clean cloth without applying any more product, and photograph the marks and the cupping in shade and under a light held low. Record the method you used and the time. Do not sand or re-oil, and do not promise that the marks will come out. Refer the floor to a qualified person for assessment, and tell the client the cleaning is paused.

workedExamples.situation: A sealed hallway floor has a dull traffic film along the walkway, but the boards are flat, the finish is intact and there is no pooling.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which method is suitable, and what limits do you set?
workedExamples.reasoning: This floor fits the minimal-moisture method. Use the approved pH-neutral product on a barely damp mop, work along the grain in short sections, and dry each section straight away. Test the product on a small area near the door first and check it after it dries. Record the method and the test. Do not use steam, and do not promise that the film will leave the finish looking new if the test shows a limited result.

equipmentAndPpe: Damp mop with a wringer, and microfibre pads for the mop head.
Clean microfibre cloths for drying each section.
Approved timber product for the finish, with its label and SDS on hand.
Torch or work light held low across the surface, for checking the finish.
Camera for dated condition photographs, used with the client's permission.
Gloves and eye protection as the SDS requires.

commonErrors.error: Flooding a timber floor to get it clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a barely damp mop, work in small sections, and dry each section promptly.

commonErrors.error: Using a strong stripping product or an ammonia-based cleaner on an oiled or sealed floor.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the finish first and use only a product approved for that timber and finish.

commonErrors.error: Continuing to mop a floor that shows cupping or pooling.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, dry without adding product, photograph the condition and refer it.

commonErrors.error: Sanding, recoating or re-oiling as part of a routine clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Refer finish work to a qualified finisher, and record that the work is outside the cleaning scope.

commonErrors.error: Promising that the finish will be restored or the stain removed.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the limits of the cleaning in writing, and record what the test showed.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Keep the SDS for every product you use, and make sure workers can get at it easily. The Safe Work Australia page on using safety data sheets states that copies must be kept for chemicals used in the hazardous chemical register, and that the SDS must be easily accessible to workers who use, handle or store the chemical (no date shown).
Slip and wet-surface risk: a damp floor is slippery, and the cleaning area should be marked while it dries.
Product-specific dilution, dwell time and PPE come from the product label and SDS.

Sanding, recoating and finish restoration are not covered by this lesson. Where a client asks for that work, refer it. Any licence or authority for finish work is outside this course, and completing this lesson does not provide one.

qualityStandard: The finish is identified from records or the water-drop test before cleaning, and the result is recorded.
A minimal-moisture method is used, and each section is dried promptly in the simulation.
Cupping, pooling or lifting boards stop the wet clean, and the condition is recorded and referred in the case study.
No claim is made that the finish has been restored, sealed or repaired.
documentationEvidence: Finish and condition record with the identification method and the test result.
Dated condition photographs, taken with permission, for any board damage or finish wear.
Referral record for any finish or board damage, with the client's acknowledgement.
Product test record for the approved product used.
summary: The finish decides the method, so identify it first.
Keep moisture minimal, work in small sections, and dry promptly.
Refer worn, lifting, cupped or pooled floors, and do not promise restoration.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is minimal moisture used on timber, even when the finish is sealed?
options: It makes the floor shine more, which the client will like to see
Water can get into the edges and joints and swell or stain the timber
It is faster than using a damp mop on the whole floor area
It keeps the floor warmer in the cold months of the year and the room

knowledgeChecks.question: Boards are cupping and water is pooling near a doorway. What is correct?
options: Mop harder to lift the dirt that has built up around the doorway
Stop, dry without adding product, photograph the condition and refer it
Sand the boards level, then clean them with the usual product on the day
Continue with a damp mop and a stronger product, since the boards are dirty

knowledgeChecks.question: Is sanding or re-oiling part of routine cleaning?
options: Yes, every time the floor is cleaned, to keep the shine
Yes, if the client asks for a shine on the floor
No, they are specialist finish work and are referred
Only on oiled floors, as part of the routine clean
